title: Apply knowledge of self and team in order to develop a plan to enhance team performance

lessons.title: Knowing yourself as a team member
lessons.html:
Why self-knowledge matters

On an irrigation crew, a packhouse line or a farm maintenance team, how well the team works depends on the people in it. Before you can help a team perform better, you need to understand yourself: your strengths, weaknesses, habits and the way you react to others.

Ways to understand yourself

  • Reflect: think about a recent job that went well and one that went badly. What did you do? How did you feel? What would you do differently?
  • Ask for feedback: ask your supervisor and colleagues what you do well and what you could improve. Listen without arguing.
  • Use simple self-assessment tools: questionnaires on learning style, working style or team roles can give a starting point. Treat them as a guide, not a label.

Strengths and development areas

AreaExample strengthExample development area
Technical skillGood at fault-finding on solenoid valvesUnsure about programming new controllers
CommunicationExplains clearly to new workersDoes not speak up in meetings
Work habitsAlways on timeLeaves tools lying around
AttitudeStays calm under pressureGets impatient with slower workers

Values and behaviour

Your values, such as honesty, respect and reliability, show in what you do: arriving on time, finishing jobs properly, reporting mistakes, and treating colleagues of every background, language and gender with respect. South African workplaces bring together many cultures; understanding your own assumptions helps you work well with everyone.

Managing your reactions

When something frustrates you, such as a colleague who does not pull their weight, notice your reaction before acting. Take a breath, find out the facts, and speak to the person privately and respectfully. Personal stress from home, money or health also affects work; know where to get help, such as an employee wellness programme if your employer has one.

lessons.title: Understanding the team
lessons.html:
What makes a team

A team is a group of people working together towards a shared goal, for example installing a sportsfield irrigation system on time and to standard. Members depend on each other: the trencher operator, the pipe layer, the valve installer and the person who tests the system.

Stages of team development

A well-known model (Tuckman) describes how teams grow:

StageWhat happens
FormingPeople are polite and unsure; they rely on the leader
StormingDisagreements arise about roles and ways of working
NormingThe team agrees on rules and starts to trust each other
PerformingThe team works smoothly and solves problems itself
AdjourningThe project ends and the team breaks up

Conflict in the storming stage is normal. Handled well, it leads to better ways of working.

Team roles

People naturally take different roles: some generate ideas, some organise, some check details, some keep the peace, some push for action. A strong team has a mix. Notice which roles you and others take, and which are missing.

Signs of a well-performing team

  • Clear goals that everyone understands
  • Clear roles and responsibilities
  • Open, respectful communication
  • Trust and willingness to help each other
  • Problems raised early and solved together
  • Safety rules followed by everyone

Signs of problems

  • Repeated rework or missed deadlines
  • Blaming, gossip and cliques
  • People not sharing information
  • Absenteeism and low morale
  • Safety short-cuts

Gather facts: look at job records, rework, incident reports and talk to team members. Do not rely on rumours.

lessons.title: Developing a plan to enhance team performance
lessons.html:
From observation to action

A team performance plan turns what you have learned about yourself and the team into specific actions.

Steps

  1. Identify the gap: compare current performance with what is required. Example: zones are often handed over with leaking valves, causing call-backs.
  2. Find causes: discuss with the team. Perhaps new members were never shown how to seal threaded joints, or there is no checklist for testing.
  3. Set goals: make them SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Example: "Reduce call-backs for leaking valves to zero within two months."
  4. Plan actions: who will do what, by when, with what resources.
  5. Agree with the team and supervisor: people support plans they help create.
  6. Implement and monitor: check progress regularly.
  7. Review: celebrate success, learn from what did not work, adjust the plan.

Example plan

ActionWhoBy whenMeasure
Short training on joint sealing and valve testingSenior installerEnd of week 1All crew trained, signed register
Introduce a handover checklistTeam leaderWeek 2Checklist completed for every zone
Weekly 15-minute toolbox talk on problems foundWhole teamOngoingTalks held, issues logged
Personal goal: learn controller programmingYouWithin 6 weeksProgrammes one site under supervision

Your personal contribution

Include your own development in the plan: a skill to learn, a habit to change, or a role to take on. Leading by example builds credibility.

Communicating the plan

Explain the plan simply, in a language the team understands, and keep it visible. Give recognition when targets are met.

Key points

  • Understand your own strengths, weaknesses and reactions through reflection and feedback.
  • Teams pass through forming, storming, norming and performing.
  • Look for clear goals, roles, trust and communication; base judgements on facts.
  • Set SMART goals and plan who does what by when.
  • Involve the team, monitor progress and review.
